Package io.mdudel.zenoh.purejava

Class PureJavaZenohSubscriber

java.lang.Object
io.mdudel.zenoh.purejava.PureJavaZenohSubscriber
All Implemented Interfaces:
AutoCloseable
public final class PureJavaZenohSubscriber extends Object implements AutoCloseable
Pure-Java Zenoh 1.x subscriber client. Sibling of PureJavaZenohPublisher: same builder shape, same endpoint parser, same TLS options. No JNI. No native binaries. Zero runtime dependencies beyond JDK 17.

Two ways to consume samples

  • Pull — call subscribe(String), then Subscription.take() / Subscription.poll(long, java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit) on the returned handle. Caller controls threading, backpressure is safe.
  • Push (callback) — call subscribeAndConsume(String, Consumer) or Subscription.forEach(Consumer) on the returned handle. Callback runs on a fresh daemon thread; caller returns immediately.

Under the hood both use the same Subscription primitive; the callback form is a thin wrapper around the pull queue.

Finding out what topics exist

Zenoh has no topic registry, so there is no authoritative list to fetch. What this client can do is merge several partial views, and it reports where each topic came from so a caller can weigh the evidence; see TopicSource. Three ways in, in rough order of usefulness:

  • Record continuously. Set recordTopics(true) on the builder, then call recordedTopics() whenever you like. The answer covers everything seen since start(), including topics that have since gone away, and it never blocks.
  • Ask once. listTopics(String, java.time.Duration) blocks for a bounded window and returns what it found in that window only.
  • Poll a live view. topics(String, boolean) returns a registry reflecting what exists right now, which you read with TopicRegistry.snapshot().

The older discoverTopics(String, TopicListener) and listTopicsNow(String, long) remain for callers that want the raw subscriber-declaration callbacks or one-shot snapshots.

Endpoint syntax

Identical to PureJavaZenohPublisher. Accepts both Zenoh classic proto/host:port form and URI form. Auto-detects PEM vs PKCS12 by file extension for TLS.

Threading

  • start() single-threaded (call once).
  • subscribe(String) safe from any thread — delegates to ZenohSession.declareSubscriber(KeyExpr).
  • close() idempotent from any thread; closes all live subscriptions in the order they were created.

    • discoverTopics

      public PureJavaZenohSubscriber.TopicDiscovery discoverTopics(String keyExprPattern, PureJavaZenohSubscriber.TopicListener listener) throws IOException
      Discover subscriber topics matching a key expression pattern. Sends a CURRENT_FUTURE INTEREST to the router; the listener fires once per existing DeclareSubscriber matching the pattern, then PureJavaZenohSubscriber.TopicListener.onDiscoveryComplete(), then for future subscriptions as they come and go.

      Note: this returns declarations SEEN BY THE ROUTER, not necessarily the set of keys anyone has ever published under. If there is no subscriber for a key, that key does not appear here even if there is an active publisher for it. To catch publishers directly, subscribe to ** with subscribeAndConsume(java.lang.String, java.util.function.Consumer<io.mdudel.zenoh.purejava.session.Sample>) and observe Sample.key().

      Parameters:
      keyExprPattern - KeyExpr pattern to filter on (wildcards welcome; use "**" to see everything).
      Throws:
      IOException

    • topics

      public TopicRegistry topics(String keyExprPattern, boolean observeTraffic) throws IOException
      Open a live TopicRegistry over every discovery channel this client can reach.

      Where discoverTopics(String, TopicListener) is a raw callback over subscriber declarations alone, this merges four sources into one queryable set: declared subscribers, declared queryables, liveliness tokens, and optionally the keys of messages that actually arrive. Each entry records which sources saw it, so the caller can tell "someone is listening here" from "data is flowing here". See TopicSource for what each one proves.

      If org is set on the builder it is prepended to the pattern, matching subscribe(String). Both channels use the same resulting pattern.

      Setting observeTraffic declares a real subscription on the pattern. On a busy network with a broad pattern that can mean a great deal of inbound data, all of which is discarded after its key is noted. It may also be refused by an ACL that allows discovery but not subscription. Pass false to stay purely passive.

      The caller owns the returned registry and must TopicRegistry.close() it. Closing this subscriber also closes any traffic subscription the registry opened.

      Parameters:
      keyExprPattern - key expression pattern to watch; "**" for everything
      observeTraffic - true to also subscribe and record observed keys
      Throws:
      IOException

    • topics

      public TopicRegistry topics(String keyExprPattern, boolean observeTraffic, boolean cumulative) throws IOException
      As topics(String, boolean), but with a choice of live or cumulative bookkeeping.

      A live registry answers "what is out there now" and drops a topic once its last declaration is withdrawn. A cumulative one answers "what has been out there since I started" and never drops anything; departed topics stay in the snapshot with TopicInfo.active() false. Observed traffic is sticky either way.

      For a cumulative registry that lives as long as the subscriber does, prefer startRecordingTopics() or the recordTopics builder flag, which own the lifecycle for you.

      Parameters:
      cumulative - true to accumulate, false to track live state
      Throws:
      IOException

    • listTopics

      public List<TopicInfo> listTopics(String keyExprPattern, Duration timeout) throws IOException
      Blocking convenience over topics(String, boolean): collect topics for up to timeout, then return the merged, sorted list.

      Waits for the router to finish replaying current declarations, then spends whatever remains of the budget observing live traffic, then closes everything. Traffic observation is always on here, since a caller wanting declarations only has no reason to block.

      The timeout is mandatory and there is no "complete" state to wait for instead. The declaration replay does finish, but traffic observation cannot: a topic that stays silent is indistinguishable from one that does not exist. Longer timeouts therefore find strictly more, and the result is always a lower bound.

      If the calling thread is interrupted the wait ends early, the interrupt flag is restored, and whatever was gathered so far is returned rather than discarded.

      Parameters:
      keyExprPattern - key expression pattern; "**" for everything
      timeout - how long to gather; must be positive
      Returns:
      topics sorted by key expression, never null, possibly empty
      Throws:
      IOException

    • startRecordingTopics

      public TopicRegistry startRecordingTopics() throws IOException
      Start accumulating topics for the life of this subscriber, so a later recordedTopics() reports everything seen since recording began rather than only what happens to be there at that instant.

      Uses the pattern and traffic setting from the builder (recordTopicsPattern, default "**", and recordTopicTraffic, default true). Setting the recordTopics builder flag calls this automatically from start(), which is the usual way in.

      Idempotent: calling it again while recording returns the running registry rather than opening a second one. The subscriber owns the registry and closes it in stop(), so callers should not close it themselves.

      Returns:
      the running cumulative registry
      Throws:
      IOException - if the subscriber is not started, or the router refuses the interest or the traffic subscription

    • topicRegistry

      public TopicRegistry topicRegistry()
      The always-on recorder, or null if recording was never started.

      Exposed for callers wanting TopicRegistry.awaitCurrent(java.time.Duration) or TopicRegistry.activeOnly(). Do not close it; use stopRecordingTopics().

    • recordedTopics

      public List<TopicInfo> recordedTopics()
      Every topic seen since recording started, sorted by key expression.

      Unlike listTopics(String, Duration) this does not block and does not open anything: the recorder has been listening all along, so the answer is already there. Topics that have since gone away are included with TopicInfo.active() false. Use TopicRegistry.activeOnly() on topicRegistry() for only what is still there.

      The longer the subscriber has been running, the more complete this is, which is the point: a topic that was busy an hour ago and silent now still shows up.

      Throws:
      IllegalStateException - if recording was never started, since an empty list would be indistinguishable from "found nothing"
